Marginalia are the notes, marks, drawings, symbols, or any other written additions that a reader has made in the blank spaces — the margins — of a book, manuscript, or document. When you pick up a second-hand book and notice that a previous reader has scribbled comments in the sides of the pages, underlined sentences with little annotations beside them, or drawn arrows and question marks next to certain paragraphs, you are looking at marginalia.

Think of marginalia as a reader's private conversation with a text — a record of their thoughts, reactions, and ideas, captured right there on the page as they read.
What Exactly Counts as Marginalia?

Marginalia can take many different forms. All of the following qualify:

  • Written notes and comments — agreeing, disagreeing, questioning, or adding to what the author says (e.g., "But this contradicts what he said on page 12!")
  • Marks and symbols — stars, crosses, checkmarks, asterisks, or exclamation marks placed next to important passages
  • Corrections — fixing an error in the printed text
  • Translations — when a reader writes the meaning of a foreign or difficult word in the margin beside it
  • Cross-references — "See also page 47" or "Compare with Aristotle"
  • Personal reactions — emotional responses like "Brilliant!" or "Nonsense."
  • Doodles and sketches — drawings, sometimes decorative, sometimes illustrative, sometimes completely unrelated to the text
  • Questions — things the reader didn't understand or wanted to investigate further
  • Summaries — brief notes capturing the key point of a paragraph in the reader's own words

The one defining quality that all marginalia share is location: they exist in the margins — the blank borders of a page — rather than on a separate piece of paper.
What Marginalia Is NOT

It's worth being precise here:

  • Simple underlining or highlighting alone is not marginalia — it only becomes marginalia when combined with a written note or mark in the margin.
  • Notes written in a separate notebook while reading are not marginalia; they are just notes.
  • The original printed or written text of the book is not marginalia — marginalia is always what someone adds to a text, not what's already there.
Why Do People Write Marginalia?

People write marginalia for many reasons, and the motivation tells you a lot about the kind of reader they are:

To think out loud. Many readers use the margins as a thinking space — a place to wrestle with ideas, push back against the author, or follow a train of thought sparked by the text. The act of writing helps them understand and remember.

To remember important parts. A star or a circled sentence tells the reader, "This mattered. Come back to this."

To have a dialogue with the author. Some readers argue back. They agree passionately or reject an idea entirely, writing their counter-arguments right where the original claim was made. In this sense, marginalia can be a form of intellectual debate across time.

To help others. In the days when books were rare and passed from person to person, readers would often leave notes to guide the next reader — explaining difficult words, flagging important sections, or warning against errors.

To study. Students and scholars often use marginalia as an active reading technique, breaking a text apart as they read it to improve comprehension.

For personal record-keeping. Sometimes people note where they were when they read a passage, what they felt, or what was happening in their life — turning the book into a kind of diary.
The Long History of Marginalia

Marginalia is not a modern habit. It is one of the oldest forms of written human commentary.

Medieval monks who hand-copied manuscripts in monasteries were prolific writers of marginalia. They would add religious reflections, corrections, and explanations to the texts they were copying. But they also, fascinatingly, wrote purely personal things — complaints about the cold, jokes, complaints about a dull text, tiny drawings of knights fighting snails (a recurring theme in medieval manuscripts that still puzzles historians). These casual, human scribbles in the margins of sacred texts are some of the most charming and revealing historical documents we have.

Ancient scholars annotated texts too. The great library at Alexandria, for example, produced annotated editions of classical texts where scholars added critical notes in the margins — a practice called "scholia." These marginal notes by ancient scholars are themselves now considered important historical documents.
Famous Examples of Marginalia

Some of the most celebrated marginalia in history come from great thinkers, making these annotations extraordinarily valuable:

Charles Darwin filled his copies of books with notes and arguments. His marginalia in the works he read while developing the theory of evolution give historians a direct window into how his thinking developed.

John Adams, the second President of the United States, was a ferocious annotator. He owned thousands of books and filled their margins with his opinions — often disagreeing sharply and colorfully with the authors.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge, the poet, was so well-known for his marginalia that some of his annotations were published as a work in their own right. He treated the margins of books as a literary space, writing fully developed thoughts and mini-essays there.

Mark Twain wrote marginalia laced with his characteristic wit and sarcasm, arguing with authors and occasionally mocking them in the margins.

Sylvia Plath annotated her books extensively, and her marginalia has been studied by scholars to understand how she engaged with literature as a writer herself.

In each of these cases, the marginalia transformed the books from mere objects into historical artifacts — evidence of a great mind at work.
The Significance and Value of Marginalia

Marginalia matters for several important reasons:

Historically, it is invaluable. When a famous scientist, philosopher, writer, or leader annotated a book, their marginalia gives us direct access to their private thoughts — unfiltered, spontaneous, and honest in a way that published works rarely are. It's as close as we can get to watching a great mind think.

Personally, marginalia makes a book uniquely yours. A book covered in your own annotations becomes a record of who you were when you read it — what struck you, what confused you, what you believed. If you re-read the same book ten years later, your old marginalia is like a message from your past self.

Intellectually, writing marginalia is considered by many educators to be one of the most effective ways to read actively and deeply. It forces you to engage, to evaluate, and to articulate your own thoughts — rather than passively absorbing (or forgetting) what you read.

Culturally, when books were shared, borrowed, or passed down through families, the accumulated marginalia of multiple readers turned a single book into a collective record — a layered conversation between all the people who had ever held it.
Grammar: Singular or Plural?

This is a subtle but important point. Marginalia is technically the plural form. The singular form is marginale (or sometimes marginalium), but these singular forms are almost never used in everyday English.

In practice, the word is used in two ways:

  • As a plural noun referring to multiple individual annotations: "The marginalia in this book are fascinating — there are notes on almost every page."
  • As an uncountable or collective noun referring to the body of annotations as a whole: "The marginalia left by Darwin has been studied for decades." (Here it functions like the word "furniture" — you don't say "a furniture," you refer to the whole collection.)

You will almost never need the word marginale. In practice, just use marginalia — both when speaking of one scribble and when speaking of hundreds.
Marginalia in the Digital Age

With the rise of e-books and digital reading, the concept of marginalia has shifted. Apps like Kindle allow readers to highlight passages and add digital notes, and some platforms even let you see the highlights and notes left by other readers — a kind of public, crowdsourced marginalia.

However, many readers and scholars argue that digital annotation lacks something essential. Physical marginalia is part of the object — it alters the book itself, ties a reader permanently to a specific copy, and carries the physical trace of a human presence (handwriting style, pressure of the pen, crossings-out). A digital note is clean, portable, and deletable — which makes it useful, but arguably less intimate and less historically durable.
Summary

Marginalia = notes, marks, drawings, and written additions made in the margins (the blank edges) of a page, added by a reader in response to the text.

It is one of the oldest intellectual habits in human history, practiced by everyone from medieval monks to Darwin to Sylvia Plath. It can be serious or playful, private or eventually public, ephemeral or historically priceless. Marginalia is simply what happens when a curious, engaged reader refuses to stay silent — and responds.
